1	% Section 3 — Method (Draft)
2	% OntoCoDec: Type-Valid Information Extraction
3	% via Compiled Ontology Constraints
4	
5	\section{Method}
6	\label{sec:method}
7	
8	We present OntoCoDec, a two-layer constrained decoding framework that compiles ontology schemas into token-level masks enforced during autoregressive generation.
9	The grammar layer (\S\ref{sec:grammar}) guarantees structural validity—well-formed JSON with ontology-vocabulary membership—while the semantic layer (\S\ref{sec:semantic}) enforces domain/range type constraints via a stateful entity registry.
10	We describe the problem formulation (\S\ref{sec:formulation}), each layer, and two decoding strategies (\S\ref{sec:strategies}).
11	Formal analysis of constraint composition is deferred to Section~\ref{sec:composition}.
12	
13	
14	\subsection{Problem Formulation}
15	\label{sec:formulation}
16	
17	\paragraph{IE as structured generation.}
18	Given an input text $x$, a language model generates a structured JSON output $y$:
19	%
20	\begin{equation}\label{eq:output-schema}
21	\resizebox{.88\columnwidth}{!}{$\displaystyle
22	  y = \bigl\{\texttt{entities}: [\{n_i, \tau_i\}],\; \texttt{relations}: [\{h_j, t_j, r_j, \tau^h_j, \tau^t_j\}]\bigr\}
23	$}
24	\end{equation}
25	%
26	where each entity has a name $n_i$ and type $\tau_i \in \mathcal{E}$, and each relation specifies head $h_j$, tail $t_j$, relation type $r_j \in \mathcal{R}$, and head/tail entity types $\tau^h_j, \tau^t_j$.
27	
28	\paragraph{Ontology schema.}
29	An ontology $\mathcal{O} = (\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{R}, \operatorname{dom}, \operatorname{range})$ defines entity types $\mathcal{E}$, relation types $\mathcal{R}$, and functions $\operatorname{dom}, \operatorname{range}: \mathcal{R} \to 2^{\mathcal{E}}$ specifying permitted head and tail types for each relation.
30	
31	\paragraph{Ontology compliance.}
32	A triple $(h, r, t)$ with $\operatorname{type}(h) = \tau^h$, $\operatorname{type}(t) = \tau^t$ is \emph{type-valid} w.r.t.\ $\mathcal{O}$ iff:
33	%
34	\begin{equation}\label{eq:type-valid}
35	  \tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r) \;\wedge\; \tau^t \in \operatorname{range}(r).
36	\end{equation}
37	%
38	Our goal is a decoding strategy maximizing $P(y \mid x)$ subject to ontology compliance: all triples must be type-valid under $\mathcal{O}$, and $y$ must be well-formed JSON conforming to Eq.~\eqref{eq:output-schema}.
39	
40	\paragraph{Constraint decidability.}
41	Not all ontology constraints are enforceable at every point during left-to-right generation.
42	We distinguish three classes by \emph{prefix-decidability}:
43	%
44	\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
45	  \item \textbf{Local constraints} depend only on the current token position.
46	    Entity-type membership ($\tau_i \in \mathcal{E}$) and relation-vocabulary membership ($r_j \in \mathcal{R}$) are local.
47	  \item \textbf{Prefix-decidable constraints} depend on previously generated context.
48	    Domain/range constraints are prefix-decidable: once head type and relation type are generated, valid tail types are fully determined.
49	  \item \textbf{Non-local constraints} depend on information not yet generated (e.g., forward coreference) and fall outside single-pass decoding.
50	\end{enumerate}
51	%
52	The grammar layer handles class~(1); the semantic layer handles class~(2).
53	
54	
55	\subsection{Grammar Layer}
56	\label{sec:grammar}
57	
58	The grammar layer compiles $\mathcal{O}$ into a context-free grammar (CFG) enforced at every decoding step via logit masking.
59	This compilation proceeds in two stages.
60	
61	\paragraph{Schema-to-grammar compilation.}
62	We generate a JSON Schema encoding the structure in Eq.~\eqref{eq:output-schema} with \texttt{enum} constraints restricting entity types to $\mathcal{E}$ and relation types to $\mathcal{R}$.
63	This schema is compiled into an EBNF grammar via XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar}, producing a pushdown automaton tracking JSON structure and enum membership.
64	
65	\paragraph{Logit masking.}
66	At step $t$, the automaton computes grammar-valid tokens $G(t) \subseteq V$; all others receive logits $-\infty$.
67	This simultaneously enforces: (i)~structural validity (well-formed JSON), (ii)~relation vocabulary membership ($r_j \in \mathcal{R}$), and (iii)~entity type membership ($\tau_i \in \mathcal{E}$).
68	Domain/range constraints are \emph{not} enforced, as they depend on entity types within each triple—the gap filled by the semantic layer.
69	
70	\paragraph{Empirical profile.}
71	On SciERC, grammar constraints eliminate relation vocabulary violations entirely (1.39\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and entity type violations entirely (0.40\%\,$\to$\,0\%), with no measurable F1 impact.
72	Domain/range violations remain effectively unchanged (15.37\%\,$\to$\,14.84\%), confirming that grammar constraints enforce structural but not semantic validity.
73	
74	
75	\subsection{Semantic Layer}
76	\label{sec:semantic}
77	
78	The semantic layer enforces domain/range constraints through a stateful logits processor maintaining an entity registry during generation.
79	
80	\subsubsection{Entity Registry}
81	\label{sec:entity-registry}
82	
83	As the model generates the entity list, the semantic layer builds a registry $\mathcal{D}: \text{name} \to \text{type}$ mapping each entity to its declared type.
84	This registry is populated incrementally: when the model completes an entry $\{n_i, \tau_i\}$, the pair $(n_i, \tau_i)$ is added to $\mathcal{D}$.
85	The registry is then consulted during relation generation to look up the declared types of head and tail entities.
86	
87	\subsubsection{Position Detection}
88	\label{sec:position-detection}
89	
90	At each step $t$, the processor determines which field is currently being generated by pattern-matching on the decoded prefix.
91	We define five field positions---\textsc{EntityType}, \textsc{RelationType}, \textsc{HeadType}, \textsc{TailType}, and \textsc{FreeText}---identified via JSON key patterns (e.g., tokens following \texttt{"head\_type":} indicate \textsc{HeadType}).
92	Semantic masks activate only at type-bearing positions (\textsc{HeadType}, \textsc{TailType}).
93	
94	\subsubsection{Dynamic Masking}
95	\label{sec:dynamic-masking}
96	
97	At type-bearing positions, the processor computes a semantic mask $S(t) \subseteq V$ restricting generation to type-valid tokens.
98	
99	\paragraph{Head type masking.}
100	At a \textsc{HeadType} position, the processor considers the entity registry $\mathcal{D}$ and the current relation type $r_j$ (if already generated).
101	If $h_j \in \mathcal{D}$ and $\mathcal{D}[h_j] \in \operatorname{dom}(r_j)$, the mask allows only that registered type: $S(t) = \{\operatorname{tok}(\mathcal{D}[h_j])\}$, ensuring consistency with both the entity list and domain constraints.
102	Otherwise, if $r_j$ is known, the mask falls back to all domain-valid types: $S(t) = \{\operatorname{tok}(\tau) : \tau \in \operatorname{dom}(r_j)\}$.
103	If $r_j$ is unavailable, no semantic mask is applied.
104	
105	\paragraph{Tail type masking.}
106	At a \textsc{TailType} position, valid tail types are computed from $\operatorname{range}(r_j)$; if $t_j \in \mathcal{D}$, the mask further restricts to the registered type when range-valid.
107	This implements the core prefix-decidable constraint: once $(h_j, r_j, \tau^h_j)$ are known, valid $\tau^t_j$ values are fully determined by $\operatorname{range}(r_j)$.
108	
109	\paragraph{Implementation.}
110	Each $\tau \in \mathcal{E}$ is mapped to the token ID of its first subword token; we pre-verify uniqueness across all entity types, which holds for both SciERC and DocRED (6 types each) with the Qwen3-8B tokenizer.
111	The semantic mask is applied by setting logits of disallowed first-token IDs to $-\infty$.
112	
113	\subsubsection{Grammar-Semantic Interaction}
114	\label{sec:interaction}
115	
116	The final mask is the conjunction of $G(t)$ and $S(t)$, permitting only tokens satisfying both layers (formalized in \S\ref{sec:composition}).
117	This embodies an \emph{enabling dependency}: semantic lookup requires relation types to be valid members of $\mathcal{R}$, guaranteed only by the grammar layer.
118	Without grammar enforcement, the model may generate out-of-vocabulary relation types for which no $\operatorname{dom}$/$\operatorname{range}$ rules exist.
119	Empirically, semantic-only constraints reduce DR by only 24\% (15.37\%\,$\to$\,11.65\%) while failing to eliminate vocabulary violations; the full combination achieves 94\% DR reduction.
120	When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$---the semantic layer would mask out all grammar-valid tokens---the system falls back to grammar-only control, preserving structural validity at the cost of a potential type violation.
121	This \emph{grammar-first invariant} reflects a deliberate priority ordering: structural integrity is a hard constraint, while type violations are soft errors detectable by downstream validation.
122	
123	
124	\subsection{Decoding Strategies}
125	\label{sec:strategies}
126	
127	\paragraph{S1: Single-pass decoding.}
128	Both constraint layers are active throughout a single generation pass.
129	The entity registry is populated as entities are generated and immediately available for relation-level type checking.
130	This is the simpler and recommended strategy, achieving strong constraint enforcement with higher relation F1 than the two-pass alternative.
131	
132	\paragraph{S2: Two-pass decoding.}\label{sec:s2}
133	The first pass generates only entities under grammar constraints; the extracted entities compile an input-dependent grammar that additionally constrains head and tail names to match declared entities.
134	The second pass generates relations under this tighter grammar plus semantic constraints.
135	Detailed comparison is provided in the appendix.

2	
3	**Date**: 2026-05-15
4	**Reproduced from**: server `westd-16980`, project `/root/schema_semantic_constrained_ie/`

7	---
8	
9	## 1. CF violation definition (recap)
10	
11	For each document, build a map `mention_text(lowercased+stripped) -> {predicted_types}` from:
12	- the `parsed_output.entities` list (after `normalize_type` filtering — invalid types are dropped first)
13	- the `head/tail` text and `head_type/tail_type` fields of every parsed relation
14	
15	A CF violation is a single `(doc_id, mention)` whose normalized type-set has cardinality > 1. The reported count is the **number of such (doc_id, mention) records**, *not* the number of pairwise conflicts. So a mention with three types is counted as one violation, but contributes one entry to the table under the sorted tuple of all its types (e.g. `Generic & Method & Task`).
16	
17	## 2. SciERC full_s1 (Qwen-2.5-7B, primary table)
18	
19	Source: `outputs/phase2_scierc_full_s1_v2.jsonl` (551 docs).
20	Total CF violations = **245** (every conflict has exactly 2 types — no 3+ -way conflicts).
21	
22	### Complete distribution (15 unique type-pair sets)
23	
24	| Rank | Conflicting type pair | Count | % of 245 |
25	|------|----------------------|------:|---------:|
26	| 1 | Generic & OtherScientificTerm | **85** | 34.7% |
27	| 2 | Generic & Material | 35 | 14.3% |

46

55	## 3. Semantic interpretation of the top pairs
56	
57	1. **Generic ↔ OtherScientificTerm (85, 34.7%).** SciERC's `Generic` is reserved for pronominal / placeholder references ("this approach", "the method", "it", "ours"). `OtherScientificTerm` is the catch-all for any scientific noun phrase that does not fit Task/Method/Material/Metric. The boundary is annotation-policy-driven, not lexically distinctive: the same surface form (e.g. "met", "system", "framework") flips between Generic when used anaphorically and OtherScientificTerm when used as a content term. The model has no in-document coreference signal to decide.
58	2. **Generic ↔ Material (35) / Generic ↔ Metric (30).** Same Generic ambiguity, now flipping against Material ("dataset", "corpus") and Metric ("score", "accuracy"). Together with row 1, these three pairs account for 150/245 (61.2%) and share a single root cause: `Generic` is a soft anaphoric label that competes with every content type.
59	3. **Method ↔ Task (20, 8.2%).** A genuinely hard ontological distinction in SciERC ("parsing", "classification", "segmentation" are sometimes a Task being solved, sometimes the Method used). This is the conflict that *cannot* be eliminated by better disambiguation — SciERC's gold annotators also disagree on these.
60	4. **Material ↔ Method (17) / OtherScientificTerm ↔ Task (12) / Method ↔ OtherScientificTerm (8).** Boundary noise between adjacent content types; lower-frequency tail.

**Date**: 2026-05-15
**Reproduced from**: server `westd-16980`, project `/root/schema_semantic_constrained_ie/`
**Checker**: `violation_checker.py` (`fixed_20260514_v2 (strip + alias + unique_et)`) / `violation_checker_docred.py`

---

## 1. CF violation definition (recap)

For each document, build a map `mention_text(lowercased+stripped) -> {predicted_types}` from:
- the `parsed_output.entities` list (after `normalize_type` filtering — invalid types are dropped first)
- the `head/tail` text and `head_type/tail_type` fields of every parsed relation

A CF violation is a single `(doc_id, mention)` whose normalized type-set has cardinality > 1. The reported count is the **number of such (doc_id, mention) records**, *not* the number of pairwise conflicts. So a mention with three types is counted as one violation, but contributes one entry to the table under the sorted tuple of all its types (e.g. `Generic & Method & Task`).

## 2. SciERC full_s1 (Qwen-2.5-7B, primary table)

Source: `outputs/phase2_scierc_full_s1_v2.jsonl` (551 docs).

| Rank | Conflicting type pair | Count | % of 245 |

| 1 | Generic & OtherScientificTerm | **85** | 34.7% |
| 2 | Generic & Material | 35 | 14.3% |
| 3 | Generic & Metric | 30 | 12.2% |

**Note on the "60" figure in the original brief.** The number 60 corresponds to *full_s2*, not full_s1: full_s2 has 60 Generic & OtherScientificTerm out of 179 total CF violations (33.5%). For full_s1 (the cell explicitly asked about in Q7), the actual count is 85 / 245 = 34.7% — confirmed by re-running the checker on the JSONL output. The qualitative claim ("Generic-vs-something dominates") holds in both modes.

### Aggregating by "involves Generic"

| Slice | Count | % of 245 |
|-------|------:|---------:|
| Conflicts involving **Generic** (rows 1, 2, 3, 13, 15) | 155 | **63.3%** |
| Conflicts involving **OtherScientificTerm** | 119 | 48.6% |

| Purely Method ↔ Task family (rows 4, 5, 6, 7, 10) | 63 | 25.7% |
| Metric-related (rows 9, 11, 12, 14) | 20 |  8.2% |

## 3. Semantic interpretation of the top pairs

1. **Generic ↔ OtherScientificTerm (85, 34.7%).** SciERC's `Generic` is reserved for pronominal / placeholder references ("this approach", "the method", "it", "ours"). `OtherScientificTerm` is the catch-all for any scientific noun phrase that does not fit Task/Method/Material/Metric. The model has no in-document coreference signal to decide.

3. **Method ↔ Task (20, 8.2%).** A genuinely hard ontological distinction in SciERC ("parsing", "classification", "segmentation" are sometimes a Task being solved, sometimes the Method used). This is the conflict that *cannot* be eliminated by better disambiguation — SciERC's gold annotators also disagree on these.
4. **Material ↔ Method (17) / OtherScientificTerm ↔ Task (12) / Method ↔ OtherScientificTerm (8).** Boundary noise between adjacent content types; lower-frequency tail.

The remainder (rows 8–15, 38 violations total) are sparse cross-content-type confusions with no single dominant pattern.

Same CF-violation accounting, applied to every available `full_s1` run plus its `unconstrained` baseline.

**Pair-based check 已在代码中实现，论文描述偏宽松。**

### head_type masking (`type_mask_processor.py` `_mask_head_type`)
```python

```
仅看 `dom(r)`，与 tail 无关 → **independent check** on head side.

### tail_type masking (`type_mask_processor.py:323` `_mask_tail_type`)
```python
if head_type is not None:
    allowed_dr = constraint.valid_tail_types_for_head(head_type)
else:
    allowed_dr = constraint.valid_tail_types()
```
其中 `valid_tail_types_for_head(head_type)` 在 `ontology_compiler.py:38` 定义为：
```python
def valid_tail_types_for_head(self, head_type: str) -> set[str]:
    return {t for h, t in self.valid_pairs if h == head_type}
```
即：在 head_type 已确定的条件下，仅允许 `σ(r)` 中以该 head_type 为头的 valid tail types。

# W3/W6 Runtime Overhead Report

**Purpose:** Reviewer W3/W6 asked for the inference-time overhead of constrained decoding. This report extracts per-document inference times from the experimental JSONL outputs and computes overhead vs. the unconstrained baseline for each (model, dataset) cell.

**Data source:** `/root/schema_semantic_constrained_ie/outputs/*.jsonl` on `westd-16980`. Every record carries an `inference_time_seconds` field written by the eval driver, so timings are read directly from the original runs—no re-runs required.

**Hardware:** All runs executed on the same single-GPU server (`westd-16980`) under the same vLLM/transformers stack, so cross-mode comparisons within a (model, dataset) pair are apples-to-apples.

---

## 1. Headline Table

Per-document inference time (seconds), wall-clock total (minutes), and overhead vs. the unconstrained baseline of the matching (model, dataset).

| Qwen  | DocRED  | grammar_only  |  998 |  20.576 |     18.730 |      342.25 | **+4.2 %**     |
| Qwen  | DocRED  | full_s1       |  998 |  20.395 |     18.812 |      339.23 | **+3.2 %**     |

3	At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
4	The final mask is their conjunction:
5	%
6	\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
7	  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
8	\end{equation}
9	%
10	so a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
11	The conjunction is asymmetric: $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$, reflecting the enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:method})---the semantic layer requires the relation type to belong to $\mathcal{R}$, a property guaranteed only by the grammar layer.
12	
13	\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
14	When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$---tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid---na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
15	We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: if no semantically valid token survives grammar filtering, semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
16	Structural integrity is a hard constraint; a type violation is a soft error detectable by downstream validation.
17	
18	\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}

At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
The final mask is their conjunction:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
\end{equation}
%
so a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.

\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$---tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid---na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: if no semantically valid token survives grammar filtering, semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
Structural integrity is a hard constraint; a type violation is a soft error detectable by downstream validation.

\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
We define the tightness of relation $r$ as:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tightness}
  \tau(r) = 1 - \frac{|\mathcal{V}(r)|}{|\mathcal{T}|^2},

%

# Q7 — Complete Distribution of Cross-Field (CF) Consistency Violations

**Date**: 2026-05-15
**Reproduced from**: server `westd-16980`, project `/root/schema_semantic_constrained_ie/`
**Checker**: `violation_checker.py` (`fixed_20260514_v2 (strip + alias + unique_et)`) / `violation_checker_docred.py`

---

## 1. CF violation definition (recap)

For each document, build a map `mention_text(lowercased+stripped) -> {predicted_types}` from:
- the `parsed_output.entities` list (after `normalize_type` filtering — invalid types are dropped first)
- the `head/tail` text and `head_type/tail_type` fields of every parsed relation

A CF violation is a single `(doc_id, mention)` whose normalized type-set has cardinality > 1. The reported count is the **number of such (doc_id, mention) records**, *not* the number of pairwise conflicts. So a mention with three types is counted as one violation, but contributes one entry to the table under the sorted tuple of all its types (e.g. `Generic & Method & Task`).

## 2. SciERC full_s1 (Qwen-2.5-7B, primary table)

Source: `outputs/phase2_scierc_full_s1_v2.jsonl` (551 docs).
Total CF violations = **245** (every conflict has exactly 2 types — no 3+ -way conflicts).

### Complete distribution (15 unique type-pair sets)

| Rank | Conflicting type pair | Count | % of 245 |
|------|----------------------|------:|---------:|
| 1 | Generic & OtherScientificTerm | **85** | 34.7% |
| 2 | Generic & Material | 35 | 14.3% |
| 3 | Generic & Metric | 30 | 12.2% |
| 4 | Method & Task | 20 |  8.2% |
| 5 | Material & Method | 17 |  6.9% |
| 6 | OtherScientificTerm & Task | 12 |  4.9% |
| 7 | Method & OtherScientificTerm | 8 |  3.3% |
| 8 | Material & OtherScientificTerm | 7 |  2.9% |
| 9 | Metric & OtherScientificTerm | 7 |  2.9% |
| 10 | Material & Task | 6 |  2.4% |

| 12 | Material & Metric | 4 |  1.6% |
| 13 | Generic & Task | 3 |  1.2% |
| 14 | Metric & Task | 3 |  1.2% |
| 15 | Generic & Method | 2 |  0.8% |
|     | **Total** | **245** | 100.0% |

**Note on the "60" figure in the original brief.** The number 60 corresponds to *full_s2*, not full_s1: full_s2 has 60 Generic & OtherScientificTerm out of 179 total CF violations (33.5%). For full_s1 (the cell explicitly asked about in Q7), the actual count is 85 / 245 = 34.7% — confirmed by re-running the checker on the JSONL output. The qualitative claim ("Generic-vs-something dominates") holds in both modes.

### Aggregating by "involves Generic"

| Slice | Count | % of 245 |
|-------|------:|---------:|
| Conflicts involving **Generic** (rows 1, 2, 3, 13, 15) | 155 | **63.3%** |
| Conflicts involving **OtherScientificTerm** | 119 | 48.6% |
| Conflicts involving **both** Generic & OtherScientificTerm | 85 | 34.7% |
| Purely Method ↔ Task family (rows 4, 5, 6, 7, 10) | 63 | 25.7% |
| Metric-related (rows 9, 11, 12, 14) | 20 |  8.2% |

## 3. Semantic interpretation of the top pairs

1. **Generic ↔ OtherScientificTerm (85, 34.7%).** SciERC's `Generic` is reserved for pronominal / placeholder references ("this approach", "the method", "it", "ours"). `OtherScientificTerm` is the catch-all for any scientific noun phrase that does not fit Task/Method/Material/Metric. The boundary is annotation-policy-driven, not lexically distinctive: the same surface form (e.g. "met", "system", "framework") flips between Generic when used anaphorically and OtherScientificTerm when used as a content term. The model has no in-document coreference signal to decide.
2. **Generic ↔ Material (35) / Generic ↔ Metric (30).** Same Generic ambiguity, now flipping against Material ("dataset", "corpus") and Metric ("score", "accuracy"). Together with row 1, these three pairs account for 150/245 (61.2%) and share a single root cause: `Generic` is a soft anaphoric label that competes with every content type.
3. **Method ↔ Task (20, 8.2%).** A genuinely hard ontological distinction in SciERC ("parsing", "classification", "segmentation" are sometimes a Task being solved, sometimes the Method used). This is the conflict that *cannot* be eliminated by better disambiguation — SciERC's gold annotators also disagree on these.
4. **Material ↔ Method (17) / OtherScientificTerm ↔ Task (12) / Method ↔ OtherScientificTerm (8).** Boundary noise between adjacent content types; lower-frequency tail.

The remainder (rows 8–15, 38 violations total) are sparse cross-content-type confusions with no single dominant pattern.

## 4. Cross-model / cross-dataset comparison

Same CF-violation accounting, applied to every available `full_s1` run plus its `unconstrained` baseline.

| Run | docs | CF total | Top-1 pair (count, %) | Top-3 share |
|-----|-----:|---------:|----------------------|------------:|
| **SciERC full_s1 (Qwen v2)**   | 551 | **245** | Generic & OtherScientificTerm (85, 34.7%) | 61.2% |
| SciERC full_s1 (Llama-3.1-8B)  | 551 | 162 | Generic & OtherScientificTerm (53, 32.7%) | 62.3% |
| SciERC full_s2 (Qwen)          | 551 | 179 | Generic & OtherScientificTerm (60, 33.5%) | 60.9% |
| SciERC unconstrained (Qwen)    | 551 |   2 | tied | — |
| SciERC unconstrained (Llama)   | 551 |   6 | Method & OtherScientificTerm (3) | — |
| DocRED full_s1 (Qwen)          | 998 | **2670** | MISC & ORG (701, 26.3%) | 58.3% |
| DocRED full_s1 (Llama)         | 998 | 3824 | NUM & TIME (671, 17.5%) | 47.4% |
| DocRED unconstrained (Qwen)    | 998 |  40 | LOC & MISC (10, 25.0%) | 70.0% |
| DocRED unconstrained (Llama)   | 998 |  78 | NUM & TIME (22, 28.2%) | 53.8% |

### Observations

1. **CF violations are an artifact of `full_s1` constrained decoding, not of the base model.**
   Both Qwen and Llama produce ≤ 10 CF violations under unconstrained decoding; constrained decoding inflates this by 1–2 orders of magnitude (245 vs. 2; 162 vs. 6; 2670 vs. 40; 3824 vs. 78). The constraint forces the model to commit to a typed prediction at each slot independently, removing the implicit cross-slot coreference that the unconstrained decoder gets for free from its prior over surface form ↔ type co-occurrence.

2. **The dominant conflict is always with the "catch-all" type.**
   In SciERC the catch-all is `Generic` (rows 1+2+3+13+15 ⇒ 63.3% of conflicts); in DocRED the catch-all is `MISC` (rows MISC&ORG, LOC&MISC, MISC&PER, MISC&NUM, MISC&TIME ⇒ 76.6% of Qwen-DocRED CF). Both catch-alls absorb low-confidence mentions, which is exactly the failure mode that creates cross-slot type drift.

3. **Llama exhibits more high-cardinality conflict sets on DocRED.**
   On DocRED full_s1, Llama produces 53 CF mentions with ≥ 3 conflicting types (and 20 with all 5 types); Qwen produces 38. This matches Llama's looser type discipline observed elsewhere in this project.

4. **DocRED `NUM ↔ TIME` (Llama, 671) and `MISC ↔ ORG` (Qwen, 701).**
   Different models lean on different shortcuts: Llama prefers TIME for any numeric-looking span (year, century), then re-classifies the same span as NUM when it appears as a relation argument whose head-role expects NUM. Qwen treats ambiguous proper nouns as MISC by default and as ORG when an organization-typing relation pulls it. Both are systematic and would benefit from per-mention type consistency at decode time.

## 5. Suggested reviewer reply (drop-in text)

> We have re-run the CF analysis on the SciERC full_s1 output (551 documents, 245 CF violations) and report the complete distribution of conflicting-type pairs in Table X. All 245 violations are pair conflicts (no mention triggered ≥ 3 types). The distribution is heavy-tailed and dominated by conflicts involving `Generic`, the type SciERC reserves for anaphoric / placeholder mentions:
>
> | Pair | Count | % |
> |------|------:|---:|
> | Generic ↔ OtherScientificTerm | 85 | 34.7% |
> | Generic ↔ Material | 35 | 14.3% |
> | Generic ↔ Metric | 30 | 12.2% |
> | Method ↔ Task | 20 | 8.2% |
> | Material ↔ Method | 17 | 6.9% |
> | (10 further pairs, each ≤ 5%) | 58 | 23.7% |
>
> Conflicts involving `Generic` account for 63.3% (155/245). This is consistent with `Generic` functioning as a soft anaphoric label in SciERC's annotation policy: the same surface form (e.g. "this approach", "the system") legitimately receives `Generic` in one mention and a content type in another, and a *per-slot* constrained decoder has no document-level coreference signal to enforce consistency. The same effect is the dominant CF mode for Llama-3.1-8B on SciERC (53/162 Generic-OtherScientificTerm, 32.7%) and shifts onto the analogous catch-all (`MISC` in DocRED) when we change ontology. Under unconstrained decoding the CF rate collapses to ≤ 1% on both datasets, confirming that CF violations are a side-effect of per-slot type commitment, not a model deficiency, and motivating the document-level consistency objective we discuss in §X.

19	The \emph{semantic layer} maintains a stateful entity registry during generation: as entities are decoded, the registry records type assignments; when relation arguments are generated, dynamic logit masking restricts output to types compatible with the relation's domain/range specification.

In a systematic study, we find violations are pervasive: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.7\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred}, driven by \emph{constraint tightness} (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology scale.

Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable---violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp.
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} guarantees syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec} (\textbf{Onto}logy-\textbf{Co}mpiled \textbf{Dec}oding), a framework that compiles an IE ontology into two composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
The \emph{grammar layer} enforces JSON well-formedness and vocabulary validity via XGrammar.
The \emph{semantic layer} maintains a stateful entity registry during generation: as entities are decoded, the registry records type assignments; when relation arguments are generated, dynamic logit masking restricts output to types compatible with the relation's domain/range specification.

\end{enumerate}
